summary: A 1970 proposed moratorium on changes to the network protocol, by R. D. Bressler. It suggests pausing changes so that implementers can build against a stable specification.

eli5.summary: The author suggests: let's stop changing the rules for a while so everyone can finish building.

questions: moratorium on changes to network protocol
why should we pause protocol changes
how to balance innovation and stability
subtitle: A call to pause protocol changes while the network becomes operational.

tldr.problem: Many RFCs propose frequent changes to the ARPANET protocol. Sites have committed 6+ months of development effort to implement the agreed protocol, and new changes force costly recoding of host and IMP software.
tldr.mechanism: Propose a 6-month moratorium on protocol changes that only improve efficiency or implementation ease. Continue to allow changes for major design flaws and protocol extensions, but freeze details.
tldr.outcome: The moratorium lets implementations stabilize, the network becomes operational faster, actual usage and operational experience will guide future improvements, and late changes do not compete with parallel network-usage development.

facts.label: Proposed moratorium length
facts.value: 6 months or until system is operational

today: RFC 72 is Unknown status. The call for a moratorium was prescient. Formal protocol change procedures (which eventually led to the RFC standards process and change control boards) were indeed needed to balance innovation with stability. Modern internet governance uses formal change procedures and semantic versioning to manage this tension.

sections.title: The Burden of Constant Changes
sections.content: Robert Bressler from MIT responds to RFC 67 (which raised concerns about marking) with a broader concern: the protocol keeps changing. Sites like MIT (Multics), Lincoln Laboratories, and others have been implementing the agreed protocol for over 6 months. Some code is complete; other parts are in advanced debugging. Each new RFC proposing a change forces developers to revise, retest, and redeploy. The effort to reprogram parts of the NCP is substantial.
sections.eli5: Software teams have been building for half a year. Every new rule change means weeks of rewriting and testing.

sections.title: The Case for Freezing Protocol Details
sections.content:
The arguments are practical, not ideological. First, getting the system operational is paramount. The real benefits of the network depend on how it is used. Development of applications and higher-layer protocols cannot proceed until the base network is working. Reprogramming effort, though greater when done later, will be hidden by parallel work on network applications.

Second, deciding what counts as an 'official change' is difficult. History shows that even settled issues are modified many times before consensus emerges. Each new suggestion can delay implementation by months as people debate and consider revisions.

Third, an idea's feasibility is unknown until actual network operation begins. Some accepted features may prove unworkable in practice; others might be reopened for change when full testing shows problems.
sections.eli5: Let's get it working first. We can learn from real use. And we should not argue forever about each small change.

sections.title: What to Freeze and What to Allow
sections.content:
Bressler proposes freezing the network protocol except in specific cases. Major design flaws should still be brought forward and discussed. Extensions to the protocol (new capabilities) can be proposed. But changes that only improve efficiency or ease of implementation should be postponed.

The intent is not to silence ideas. New proposals should still be written and debated, but with the understanding that they are 'Proposals for Post-Moratorium Changes' rather than immediate modifications. This preserves design discussion while allowing implementations to proceed.
sections.eli5: Fix real problems now. Improve efficiency later. Write down all the good ideas for after we are running.

references.text: Crowther, W. Proposed Modification to the Host-IMP Protocol.
